events.text: You stand on the highest peak of {pw_world}, higher than anyone born here has ever stood. Above you the sky goes on: no stair, no gate, no floor of cloud, nothing for a foot to rest on. The priests below say the one who made the world {pw_record}. Up here it is plain that whoever it was never built anything above it. The wind is very clean, and very lonely.

choices.text: Cut a single step into the last rock, for whoever comes next

effects.log: It takes a season. When it is done it is only one step, leading nowhere. You sit on it in the evenings. It is strange how much it feels like the beginning of something.

choices.text: Shout up into the empty sky

effects.log: Your voice goes up and does not come back. No echo: there is nothing up there to give it one. Far below, at a well, a child looks up for no reason and keeps looking.

choices.text: Climb down and live among the people

effects.log: There is nothing higher to climb, so you climb down. You spend your years among {pw_people}, who find it odd that the greatest of them mends nets and shells beans. You find it is not a bad way to be the greatest of anything.

events.text: On the bare summit of {pw_world} there is a hermit, so old the snow has stopped melting on their shoulders. They reached the top three hundred years ago and never went down. 'I am waiting for the sky to be finished,' the hermit says, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world. 'Look how few stars there are. Somebody meant to put more. Somebody meant to put stairs.'

choices.text: Keep the hermit company for a winter

effects.log: You share a fire through the long dark. The hermit names every star there is, which takes one evening, and then names the ones that should be there, which takes all winter.

choices.text: Ask what the hermit would do with a stair

effects.log: "Climb it," the hermit says. "Then thank whoever built it. Then come back down and tell everyone." The hermit looks at you sidelong. "You would do the same. I can tell. You have the face of someone who builds things."

choices.text: Leave the hermit a lamp and go

effects.log: You leave your lamp burning on the summit. Years later, in the valleys, people say there is a new star very low over the highest mountain, and it does not move.

events.text: The stairs above the top of {pw_world} are new: the cuts still sharp, the stone dust not yet blown away, though nobody alive can say when they were made. At the top, on a floor of cloud, a small grey figure is sweeping with a broom of reeds. 'Mind the forty-first step,' they say without looking up. 'It rocks. It has rocked since the day it was cut. The one who cut it meant to come back.' Their name is Pell. They have swept the First Sky for longer than {pw_people} have had a name.

choices.text: Take the spare broom and sweep beside Pell

effects.log: You sweep until dusk. Pell says nothing for hours, then: "You sweep like someone who has done it before." You have never swept cloud in your life. It does feel familiar.

choices.text: Ask who cut the stairs

effects.log: "The one who made everything," Pell says. "Came down this way with a chisel, cut every step in one night, went back up. Left the chisel." Pell taps a bundle of cloth tied to the broom handle. "I keep it. Somebody should."

choices.text: Press the forty-first step back into place

ok.log: You find the angle the stone wants, the way you find a word on the tip of your tongue, and it stops rocking. Pell stares at it, and then at you, for a long time.

fail.log: It will not sit. Whatever it needs, you do not have it yet. Pell pats your arm. "Nobody can," they say. "Only the one who cut it."

events.text: The floor of the First Sky gives under your feet like new snow, and holds. Across it, toward a haze where more stairs must be, runs a line of old footprints pressed into the cloud and never filled. They are exactly the size of yours. A grey little sweeper called Pell leans on a broom and watches you notice them. 'Nobody walks in those,' Pell says. 'Out of respect. Though nobody remembers for whom.'

choices.text: Walk in the footprints

effects.log: Every step fits. Halfway along you realise you are matching the stride too, a long, patient stride you have never used in your life. Behind you, Pell has stopped sweeping.

choices.text: Walk beside them, making your own

effects.log: Your line of prints runs beside the old one all the way to the haze. Next morning Pell has swept yours away and left the old ones, but has swept a little path between them, as if the two should be able to meet.

choices.text: Ask Pell who made them

effects.log: "Someone going up," Pell says, "who never came back down. That is all footprints ever tell you." Then, after a moment: "They had a chisel. I kept it."

events.text: The Cloud Court of {pw_world} is a hall of mist held up by nothing, and around it in a great ring stand the seats of its gods. A herald of mist with no face asks your name, and then, politely, what you are the god of. When you say you are not a god at all, the whole court turns to look at you, as people look at a bird that has flown in through a window.

choices.text: Give your name and nothing else

effects.log: The herald writes it on the air, where it hangs among the names of gods. It looks very small there. Nobody wipes it away.

choices.text: Say: "Nothing yet."

effects.log: A few of the gods laugh. One does not: an old god at the far end of the ring leans forward, as if those two words had been the password to something.

choices.text: Ask whose is the seat at the very top, with nobody in it

effects.log: The herald's mist goes still. "That is not a seat of this court," it says. "That is higher. Nobody goes there." And then, more quietly: "Nobody has yet."

events.text: Your first night in the Cloud Court there is a feast, and you are placed at the lowest table among the lamp-spirits. At the head of the hall, at an empty place, a cup is poured and left full, as it is at every feast. 'For the one who made us,' the herald whispers. 'Who never comes.' Nobody has touched that cup in all the {pw_years} years of the world.

choices.text: Leave it alone, as everyone does

effects.log: You eat with the lamp-spirits, who are good company and very warm. When the feast ends the cup is still full. For a moment, from the bottom of the hall, you could swear it was full for you.

choices.text: Walk up and refill the full cup

effects.log: You pour, and the cup takes it without spilling a drop, as if it had been waiting to be filled for a very long time. The court falls silent. Then, one by one, the gods raise their own cups toward the empty place.

choices.text: Raise it

ok.log: You raise it to the hall and pour it on the cloud, as a maker should. It smells of the first spring of the world. Nobody stops you. Afterwards nobody can say why nobody stopped you.

fail.log: The god of the nearest seat catches your wrist, not unkindly, and the wine spills on the cloud. "Not that one," they say. "Anything but that one."

events.text: Above the Cloud Court the stairs turn green, and you come into the Jade Vault: room after room of green stone where {pw_world} keeps what it has not used yet. On one shelf, a colour nobody below has ever seen, folded small. In a drawer, a season with no name. In a jar, a song meant for a people not yet made. At the end of the last room is a drawer marked, in a hand you almost know, 'for later'.

choices.text: Open the drawer marked "for later"

effects.log: Inside is a single seed, a folded map of the world with one valley left blank, and a note that says only: "When you are ready." You close it again. You do not know why your hands are shaking.

choices.text: Unfold the colour nobody has seen, just for a moment

effects.log: For a moment the room is a colour there is no word for. When you fold it away you are close to tears and could not say why. Somewhere far below, a painter of {pw_kingdom} wakes from a dream and cannot remember it.

choices.text: Touch nothing. None of it is yours

effects.log: You walk through every room with your hands behind your back. At the door, oddly, you feel the Vault is disappointed, the way a house is when its owner walks past it in the street.

events.text: Quill, the keeper of the Jade Vault, is a spirit of green stone with ink on every finger, and keeps the ledger of everything in {pw_world} not yet used. 'Name?' Quill asks, and finds you in the ledger at once, which surprises you both. The entry is very old. It says: 'One life, to be lived from the inside. Not yet used.' Then it has been struck through, and beside it, in fresh ink, someone has written: 'In use.'

choices.text: Ask who wrote the entry

effects.log: "The one who made us," Quill says. "Every entry in this book is in that hand." Quill turns the ledger round. It is a stranger's writing. It is also, somehow, the way you would write if you were very tired and very sure.

choices.text: Ask to be struck out of the ledger

effects.log: Quill refuses, gently. "Everything in this Vault is waiting to be used," Quill says, "or being used. There is no third kind of thing."

choices.text: Help Quill count the Vault for a season

effects.log: You count unmade seasons and unsung songs until your eyes ache. Quill says you are the fastest clerk the Vault has ever had, and the only one, and asks you to stay. You almost say yes.

events.text: The last stairs are the shortest. At the top, the Ninth Heaven of {pw_world}: a hall with no walls, open on every side to the dark, and below it the whole world turning slowly, small enough to cover with your hand. At the far end, on three low steps, an empty throne of pale stone. On the last step sits Pell, the sweeper of the First Sky, broom across their knees. 'I followed you,' Pell says. 'I have never been this high. I wanted to see who it was for.'

choices.text: Sit with Pell on the bottom step

effects.log: You sit. Pell unwraps the chisel at last and shows you: old iron, worn to the shape of one hand. "I always thought I would know them when they came back," Pell says. "I thought they would look like a god."

choices.text: Walk all the way round the throne

effects.log: There is no dust on it, though there is dust everywhere else. On the back, low down, where only someone sitting could reach, is a single chisel scratch: the kind of mark a maker leaves to say, this one is mine.

choices.text: Look down at the world instead

effects.log: From here {pw_world} is a map that breathes. You find the valley where you were born without looking for it, the way a hand finds a pocket. It looks very small. It looks very loved.

events.text: In the Ninth Heaven the floor is not cloud but glass, and under the glass, very small, are the names of everyone who has ever lived in {pw_world}, all {pw_years} years of them, in the order they were born. The newest are still being written as you watch, by no hand. You find your own name. Beside every other name there is a line and a date. Beside yours there is only a small mark you do not understand: a single chisel scratch.

choices.text: Kneel and read the names around yours

effects.log: They are the people of your village, your street, your childhood. You remember all of them. It is strange to find them written in heaven, and stranger that it does not feel strange.

choices.text: Follow the names back to the first one ever written

ok.log: You follow them back across the whole floor, to the foot of the empty throne. The first name is not a name at all. It is the same chisel scratch that stands beside yours.

fail.log: The names go back further than your eyes can follow. You lose your place at the foot of the throne's steps, and decide that perhaps you were not meant to read that far yet.

choices.text: Leave the names to their writing

effects.log: You step carefully between them to the edge of the hall, as you would through a field someone else had sown.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of the Harvest, finds you on a terrace of {pw_hv_tier} and puts a loaf in your hands without a word. It is warm. 'From the first field anybody ever sowed in {pw_world},' they say. 'I keep a corner of it going up here. Nobody prays for it any more. I do it anyway.' Then, peering at you: 'You look like someone who has not eaten properly since the day you were born.'

choices.text: Eat, and say it is the best bread you have ever had

effects.log: It is. {pw_hv_god} beams, and from then on there is a loaf at your door every morning, still warm, wrapped in a cloth that smells of rain on earth.

choices.text: Ask to work the heavenly field

effects.log: You work the little field all season beside the god, who talks the whole time about rain. At harvest the god sends one sheaf down to {pw_world}, and that year no village of {pw_people} goes hungry.

choices.text: Save half the loaf for later

effects.log: {pw_hv_god} nods approvingly. "Someone taught you that," they say. "The one who made us used to say it: keep back one seed. I never knew for what."

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of the Harvest, is weighing grain on a scale of cloud when you pass, and calls you over without looking up. 'You came up from below. Tell me straight. Do they still leave the first sheaf at the edge of the field for the gods, down there? Or has that gone the way of everything?' The scale wobbles. The god is watching the scale, not you.

choices.text: Tell the truth: some do, most do not

effects.log: The god sighs, and the scale settles. "Some," they say. "Some is a harvest. I can work with some." You understand that you have been weighed, and found honest.

choices.text: Say: "All of them. Every field."

effects.log: The scale tips hard. The god looks at you at last, says nothing, and goes back to weighing. That season a little less rain falls on {pw_world}, as if someone had been told a pleasant lie and resented it.

choices.text: Promise to leave the first sheaf yourself, next harvest

effects.log: At harvest you go down and leave a sheaf at the edge of a field of {pw_people}, and come back up with straw in your hair. The god never mentions it. But your bowl in {pw_hv_tier} is never empty again.

events.text: The terraces of {pw_hv_god}, god of the Harvest, are bare: furrows of cloud with nothing in them, a plough left where it stopped. The god sits in the dust of the last field. 'The one who made us gave me the harvest,' they say, 'and went away, and never once asked how it grew. So I stopped growing it.' They hold out a single grain. 'You think you are something, climbing up here. Make that grow. On cloud. Then we will talk.'

choices.text: Plant the grain and tend it, however long it takes

ok.log: It takes a year. You water it with your own qi and sit up with it on cold nights. In spring there is one green blade in the dead field. The god stares at it, and then, roughly, gets up and fetches the plough.

fail.log: The grain sleeps in the cloud and will not wake, however much of yourself you pour into it. The god takes it back. "No," they say, not unkindly. "It never does. Not for anyone."

choices.text: Ask what they grew, before they stopped

effects.log: Nobody has asked in an age. The god talks until dark: barley like gold wire, a melon so sweet it made a king weep, a rice that grew in snow. At the end they are almost smiling, and angry at themselves for it.

choices.text: Tell them it is none of your business

effects.log: "No," the god agrees. "It never was anyone's." That autumn the harvest of {pw_world} comes in thin.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of War, turns out to be stooped and grey and very tired, and keeps a table in {pw_hv_tier} with a map of {pw_world} on it, covered in little stone figures. 'Every battle there has ever been,' they say. 'I remember each one. Nobody else wants to.' They push a cup of something bitter across to you. 'You have the look of someone who has had to fight. Sit. I could use the company of someone who is not a soldier.'

choices.text: Sit, and let the old god tell the battles

effects.log: They tell them all, through the night, and the names of the fallen in each: not the generals, the fallen. At dawn the god sweeps half the little figures off the map into a box, very gently. "Those I can put away now," they say. "Somebody else has heard them."

choices.text: Ask to be taught

effects.log: The god teaches you for a season, and it is not what you expected. It is how to see a fight coming three years off, how to end it in one day, and how to stand so that the other side can stand down without shame.

choices.text: Ask why a god of war is so sad

effects.log: "Because I am good at it," the god says. "And the one who made me never said what I was for. I have been guessing for {pw_years} years."

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of War, blocks a corridor of mist with a spear held across it, and looks you up and down. 'Strangers do not climb this heaven,' they say. 'Either you are a hero, or you are a spy for the thing that hunts in our halls. Show me which. One pass. I will not hold back much.'

choices.text: Take the pass

ok.log: You meet the spear and turn it, and for one moment the god is off balance. They laugh, a soldier's bark. "Hero, then," they say, and lift the spear out of your way.

fail.log: The butt of the spear finds your ribs and you sit down hard on the cloud. The god helps you up. "Not a spy," they say. "A spy would have known better than to try."

choices.text: Refuse to fight a god who is only guarding their home

effects.log: The spear lowers by a hand's width. "That," says the god, "is the right answer, and nobody ever gives it." They step aside.

choices.text: Go round by another hall

effects.log: It takes you all day. The god of War is waiting at the other end, arms folded, and gives you a nod that might be respect and might be amusement.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of War, has not been prayed to properly in a long age, and it has made them hard. They meet you on the parade ground of {pw_hv_tier} with a hundred soldiers of cloud drawn up behind them. 'The one who made me gave me war and then left me no one to fight but the dark,' they say. 'You will do. Kneel and serve in my ranks, or stand and be tried.'

choices.text: Stand and be tried

ok.log: You stand all day against the soldiers of cloud, and do not kneel, and never strike to kill. At sunset the god dismisses the ranks. "At last," they say, "something in this heaven that will not bend."

fail.log: The soldiers of cloud bear you down by sheer number. You do not kneel, but you do fall. The god looks at you lying there. "Better," they say, "than most."

choices.text: Kneel, and ask to serve

effects.log: You drill in the god's ranks for a season. At the end of it they know your name and you know theirs, and that turns out to be worth more than you expected.

choices.text: Tell them a soldier without a war should be glad

effects.log: The god's face goes dark. "Glad," they repeat. "Glad, and forgotten." They turn their back on you, and the ranks of cloud march away into the mist.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of Healing, catches your hand as you pass and turns it over. 'Every scar,' they say, delighted, 'tells me a story. Sit, sit.' They read your old hurts like a letter: a fall you had forgotten, the fever of a bad winter, the long mark of a hard year. Their fingers are cool. Where they touch, the old aches go out like lamps at dawn.

choices.text: Let them heal all of it

effects.log: You walk away lighter than you have been since you were small. The god writes your scars down in a little book. "For the record," they say. "Somebody ought to remember what a body has been through."

choices.text: Ask them to leave one scar

effects.log: The god smiles, as if you had answered a question they had not asked aloud. "The one who made us said that too," they say. "Leave one, so you know you were there."

choices.text: Ask what they cannot heal

effects.log: "Grief," the god says, "and pride, and a world whose maker has gone quiet." They close your hand for you. "Those three I only tend."

events.text: A fever is moving through a town of {pw_people} far below, and {pw_hv_god}, god of Healing, is watching it through a gap in the cloud, hands folded, not moving. 'I could stop it,' they say, when you kneel beside them. 'It would cost me a season of my strength. I am not sure they would notice. I am not sure the one who made us would notice. Would you?'

choices.text: "I would. Stop it."

effects.log: The god looks at you a long moment, then reaches down through the gap. The fever breaks in a single night. The god is grey and shaking for months after, and every morning you bring them broth, and they say it is the first thing anyone has ever done for them.

choices.text: Lend them your own strength for it

effects.log: You put your hands on the god's shoulders and give. Together you reach down, and the fever goes out of the town like a tide. You are both ill for a season, side by side, and laugh about it.

choices.text: Tell them it is their choice, not yours

effects.log: The god nods slowly and does nothing. The fever runs its course. Afterwards the god does not look at you, or at the gap in the cloud, for a long time.

events.text: The house of {pw_hv_god}, god of Healing, is shut, and the herbs on its doorstep are dead. You knock. The door opens a crack. 'The one who made us made everything able to break,' the god says, 'and then left me to mend it, alone, for ever. I am tired of mending.' On the step lies a heron of cloud with a broken wing. 'If you are so clever, stranger, you mend it.'

choices.text: Set the heron's wing with what you know

ok.log: You splint it with reed and a strip of your own sleeve and sit with it through the night. At dawn it flies, crookedly. The door opens wider. The god comes out to watch it, and does not go back in.

fail.log: The wing will not set under your hands. The god takes the heron and mends it in a breath, and looks at you with something less than scorn. "At least you tried," they say. "That is more than some."

choices.text: Sit on the step and wait until they come out

effects.log: You wait three days. On the fourth the god comes out with two cups of tea and sits beside you, the heron between you, and says nothing at all, and that is the beginning.

choices.text: Leave. Nobody should be bullied into kindness

effects.log: You go. Behind you the door shuts. That winter there is more sickness in {pw_world} than there has been for an age.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of Wisdom, keeps a library in {pw_hv_tier} with a book for every thought anyone in {pw_world} has ever had. 'Most of them are about lunch,' the god admits cheerfully, letting you in. 'But some!' They pull down a slim one bound in blue. 'The first time anybody below wondered who made them. A shepherd on a hill. I read it on bad days.'

choices.text: Read the shepherd's book

effects.log: It is one page long. It ends with a question mark, and then, in a different ink, as if somebody came later and answered it, a single chisel scratch.

choices.text: Ask for the books of your own thoughts

effects.log: The god searches, and searches, and comes back puzzled. "Your shelf is here," they say. "But the oldest books on it are written in a hand older than you. Older than me."

choices.text: Offer to help shelve

effects.log: You shelve for a season. The god talks the whole time, gloriously, and by the end you have read half the minds of {pw_world} and like them better than you expected.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of Wisdom, stops you on a bridge of mist and asks you a question, as is their right. 'What,' they say, 'does a maker owe the thing it made?' They wait. They are known to wait a hundred years for a good answer.

choices.text: "Attention."

effects.log: The god considers this for a month. Then they write it on the rail of the bridge, where every god who crosses will read it, and go away looking troubled.

choices.text: "Nothing. A gift owes nothing back."

effects.log: "Then is a world a gift?" the god asks, and you find you cannot answer, and the god is pleased with you for not pretending.

choices.text: "To come back."

effects.log: The god goes very still. "Yes," they say at last. "That is what every one of us thinks, up here, and none of us says." They let you pass, and watch you a long way.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of Wisdom, has burned most of their books. The rest are stacked like a wall around their seat. 'The one who made us left no word,' they say. 'No reason, no note. I read everything in this world looking for one line from them, and there was none. So: a test, since you think you are wise enough to climb. Three riddles. Fail, and you go back down the stairs.'

choices.text: Answer the riddles

ok.log: The third riddle is: what does a maker leave behind? You say: the world. The god sits a long time behind their wall of books, and then begins, slowly, to take it down.

fail.log: You miss the second. The god does not send you down after all. "Nobody gets the second," they say, tired. "I do not know the answer myself."

choices.text: Tell them the world itself is the note

effects.log: The god laughs, harshly, and then stops laughing. That night their lamp burns late, and in the morning they are reading a farmer's almanac from {pw_kingdom} as though it were scripture.

choices.text: Refuse to be tested by a sulking god

effects.log: The god turns back to their ashes. Below, that year, the schools of {pw_world} quarrel bitterly, and nobody can remember why.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of the Dead, keeps a garden of lanterns in {pw_hv_tier}, one for every soul of {pw_world} that has gone on, and walks you through it as gently as through a sickroom. 'Anyone you would like to see?' they ask. 'They cannot speak. But the light is theirs.' Among the lanterns, one burns with a colour you know at once.

choices.text: Sit by the lantern you know

effects.log: You sit there until the god comes to tell you it is morning. The light leans toward you a little the whole time, the way a person leans across a table. You do not cry until much later.

choices.text: Ask why the lantern at the heart of the garden is unlit

effects.log: "That one is for the one who made us," the god says, "for when they die, if they can. I have kept it trimmed for {pw_years} years." They look at you, and then away, as if they had said too much.

choices.text: Help trim the lanterns

effects.log: It is quiet, gentle work. By the end of the season the god has shown you all their favourites, and you have learned that the dead of {pw_world} are mostly remembered for small kindnesses.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of the Dead, keeps the ferry over the river of mist between {pw_hv_tier} and whatever comes after. They do not offer you a seat. 'You are not dead,' they say. 'That is unusual, this high. Most who come up here are only passing through on their way out. What do you want of me?'

choices.text: Ask to cross, only to look, and come back

ok.log: The ferry takes you out to the middle and turns back. What you see over there you never quite describe, even to yourself. It is not frightening. It is very large, and it is waiting to be finished.

fail.log: Halfway across, the mist goes cold in your chest, and the god turns the ferry round without a word. "Not yet," they say. "You are not done."

choices.text: Ask what the dead of the world say about the one who made it

effects.log: "They forgive them," the god says. "Every one. It surprised me at first. I suppose when you have finished living a life, you understand that somebody had to give it to you."

choices.text: Ask for nothing, and leave the ferry be

effects.log: The god nods, almost warmly. "Most who come want something," they say. "Come back when you do not want anything. I will have a seat for you then."

events.text: The ferry of {pw_hv_god}, god of the Dead, is drawn up on a shore of mist, and the god sits on its rail, hollow-eyed. The dead have been crossing without a ferryman for a long time. 'The one who made us made death,' they say, 'and gave it to me, and never once sat with me while I did it.' They put the pole in your hands. 'Ferry one soul across. If you can bear it, you can stay.'

choices.text: Take the pole and ferry one soul

ok.log: The soul is an old farmer of {pw_people} who talks about plum trees the whole way over. On the far shore they pat your hand and go. When you come back, the god is standing for the first time in an age.

fail.log: The mist is too heavy for you; the soul has to help you steer, and by the far shore you are both laughing in a way neither of you expected. The god takes the pole back, almost gently.

choices.text: Offer to sit with the god while they do it

effects.log: You sit in the bow all season while the god ferries the dead of {pw_world}. You talk about nothing. At the end the god says it was the shortest season in {pw_years} years.

choices.text: Refuse to touch the pole

effects.log: The god lets the pole drift away in the mist. Below, the dead of {pw_world} wait a little longer on the shore than they should, and the people who loved them feel it as a cold wind.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of Fate, sits at a loom as wide as {pw_hv_tier}, weaving the lives of {pw_world} into a cloth that runs off the edge and down into the world. They wave you over, delighted to have company. 'Find yourself,' they say. 'Go on. Everybody wants to.' You look. Every thread in the world is there. Yours is not.

choices.text: Ask where your thread is

effects.log: The god searches the cloth from end to end and goes quiet. "There is a hole," they say at last, "exactly your shape. It has been there since the first row. I thought it was a mistake. I have woven around it for {pw_years} years."

choices.text: Sit at the loom and weave one row

ok.log: Your row comes out even and bright. The god holds it to the light and whistles. "You weave like someone who drew the pattern," they say.

fail.log: You tangle three lives together, and the god spends an evening getting them apart. Somewhere below, three strangers meet at a crossroads and become friends for life, and the god decides to leave it.

choices.text: Ask them not to show you anything

effects.log: The god throws a cloth over the loom at once, pleased. "Most people beg," they say. "It is so much better not to know."

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of Fate, stops you in a hall of mist and holds up a single thread, pale and fraying at one end. 'This is how your life ends,' they say. 'I can tell you when. I can tell you how. People always think they want to know. Do you?'

choices.text: "Tell me."

ok.log: The god looks at the frayed end a long time and puts it away. "It does not say," they admit. "It just stops, at the top of a stair. As if somebody had not decided yet."

fail.log: The god tells you. You forget it at once, completely, and are glad, and the god looks relieved, as if the forgetting had been the test.

choices.text: "No. Put it away."

effects.log: "Good," says the god, and puts it away. "Most people who know the end stop living the middle."

choices.text: Ask whose hands spun that thread

effects.log: "Not mine," the god says, frowning at it. "Every other thread in the world, mine. This one came already spun."

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of Fate, has let the loom run wild. Lives below are tangling: the wrong people meeting, the right ones missing each other by a single street. 'Why should I weave carefully,' the god says, 'for a maker who never once looked at the pattern?' They hand you the shears. 'You want to prove you are something? Cut it straight. Choose where.'

choices.text: Cut the knot, not a thread

ok.log: You find the knot where it all went wrong and cut that, and the threads fall apart into their right places. The god stares at the loom. "Nobody ever thinks of that," they say. "I never thought of that."

fail.log: You cut the wrong knot, and the god spends a night setting it right. In the morning, oddly, they are less angry than before you came.

choices.text: Give the shears back

effects.log: "I will not cut anyone," you say. The god turns the shears over in their hands for a long time. Then they sit down at the loom and begin, very slowly, to untangle it.

choices.text: Tell them to fix it themselves

effects.log: The god throws the shears down. Below, that year, more friends of {pw_world} miss each other by a single street than in any year before.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of the Wild, comes to you as a fox the colour of evening cloud, and walks beside you for a whole day before turning into anything else. When they do, they are barefoot, burr-haired, laughing. 'You smell of the world,' they say. 'Proper world. Mud and river. Nobody up here does.' Every beast of {pw_hv_tier} seems to know them, and now, apparently, you.

choices.text: Run with the god's beasts for a season

effects.log: You run with cloud-deer and sleep in a heap of cloud-wolves and wake with leaves in your hair, though there are no trees up here. The god says you run like something that used to have four legs. You decide to take it kindly.

choices.text: Ask about the beasts of the world below

effects.log: They talk about every beast below as if it were a cousin. At the end they say, more quietly: "The one who made us made the first fox as a joke, I think. I have always been grateful."

choices.text: Ask for a beast to walk with you

effects.log: The god whistles, and a small cloud-heron lands on your shoulder and refuses ever to leave. It is no use at all, and you love it.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of the Wild, circles you on all fours, sniffing. 'Hunter?' they ask. 'Or hunted? Everything that climbs up here is one or the other.' Across a meadow of cloud a great white stag is watching you both. 'That one has never been caught. Show me what you are.'

choices.text: Run the stag down

ok.log: You run the stag across three meadows and touch its flank, and let it go. The god howls with joy. "A hunter who does not kill," they say. "Good. There are not enough of those."

fail.log: The stag leaves you face down in a bank of cloud. The god sits beside you, shaking with laughter. "Hunted, then," they say. "That is not a bad thing to be, either."

choices.text: Sit down, and let the stag come to you

effects.log: It takes all afternoon. At dusk the stag lowers its head and breathes on your hands. The god watches with an odd, guarded face, as if they had seen this once before, long ago.

choices.text: Say you are neither, and walk on

effects.log: The god cocks their head. "Everything is one or the other," they say. "Except the one who made us. Huh." They follow you a little way, curious.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of the Wild, has gone back to the wild. Their meadows in {pw_hv_tier} are overgrown with briars of cloud, and something large moves in them. 'The one who made us made the wild and left it,' says a voice from the briars. 'So the wild left too.' A pack of storm-wolves comes out of the dark, low and silent. 'Let us see if you belong up here.'

choices.text: Stand your ground without striking

ok.log: You stand, and the wolves circle, and you do not strike, and at last the lead wolf sits. The god comes out of the briars, astonished, and sits too.

fail.log: The wolves bowl you over and tear at your sleeves and leave you bruised in the briars. The god looks down at you. "You did not strike them," they say. "Why not?"

choices.text: Howl back

effects.log: You do not know why you do it. The wolves stop. In the briars the god laughs, a wild, cracked sound, the first in an age, and comes out to look at you properly.

choices.text: Run

effects.log: You get away, scratched by briars. Behind you the god says, to nobody: "Of course." Below, that year, the beasts of {pw_world} come down out of the hills hungry and bold.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of the Hearth, has a kitchen in {pw_hv_tier}, low and smoky and smelling of onions, and sits you down in it as if you were late for supper. 'You have the look,' they say, ladling soup, 'of someone a long way from home. Eat. Then tell me about the place you grew up. I like to hear about kitchens.'

choices.text: Tell them about the kitchen you grew up in

effects.log: You tell them about the smoke-black beam and the cracked pot and who sat where. The god listens with their chin in their hands. "I lit that fire," they say, when you finish. "I light all of them. It is nice to hear how one turned out."

choices.text: Wash up afterwards

effects.log: The god is so surprised they drop a ladle. Nobody has ever washed up in the kitchen of the god of the Hearth. From then on there is always a bowl kept warm for you at the back of the stove.

choices.text: Ask whether gods get homesick

effects.log: The god stirs the pot a long time. "For somebody," they say. "The one who lit me. They sat right where you are sitting, once, and then went. I keep the chair."

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of the Hearth, hands you a little clay lamp with a flame in it no bigger than a grain of rice. 'Carry it down to the poorest house in {pw_world},' they say, 'and do not let it go out. Do that, and I will know what you are. Others have tried. The wind on the stairs is cruel.'

choices.text: Carry the lamp down every stair

ok.log: You shelter it with your body all the way down, through every tier, and set it on the bare hearth of a widow of {pw_people} who had no fire that winter. When you climb back, the god of the Hearth is waiting with soup.

fail.log: On the way down the wind takes it. You stand there with the cold lamp in your hands. When you climb back, the god says: "It went out on the forty-first step, did it not? It always does. That step rocks."

choices.text: Ask why they do not carry it themselves

effects.log: "A god of the hearth cannot leave the hearth," they say. "That is the rule. The one who made us kept it too, as long as they could. Then they had to go."

choices.text: Give the lamp back: you might fail them

effects.log: The god takes it back, not offended. "Honest," they say. "Most strangers are too proud to say that."

events.text: The kitchen of {pw_hv_god}, god of the Hearth, is dark, the stove cold, a single chair pulled up to it. 'The one who made us lit me,' the god says from the shadows, 'and sat by me one night, and went away. I waited. Then I stopped waiting, and the fire went out.' They do not light a lamp for you. 'Light it, if you want to stay in my house. No flint. No qi-fire. Warmth only.'

choices.text: Sit by the cold stove and wait, as they did

ok.log: You sit all night and think about every fire you have ever sat by. Near dawn a coal you had not seen begins to glow. The god makes a sound like a sob, and comes and kneels and blows on it, and it catches.

fail.log: You sit until you are stiff with cold, and nothing catches. In the grey morning the god puts a blanket over your shoulders without a word. It is a start.

choices.text: Sit in the empty chair

effects.log: The god stiffens. Then, slowly, they come and sit on the floor beside the chair, the way someone sits by a person they have missed. Neither of you says anything. In the morning the stove is warm.

choices.text: Leave the god their dark

effects.log: You go. That winter, all over {pw_world}, fires are harder to light and go out sooner, and nobody below knows why.

events.text: In a hall of {pw_hv_tier}, {pw_hv_god}, god of {pw_hv_domain}, stops halfway through a step and turns to stare at you. Everyone up here knows they were a person once, a legend of some other world, given a seat in this heaven long ago. 'You,' they say. 'No. You cannot be. That one is gone.' Their voice is not steady. 'Hold your cup again. The way you were holding it.'

choices.text: Hold the cup again

effects.log: {pw_hv_god} watches your hands as if reading a letter in them. "The thumb," they say softly. "Just there. Someone I walked a long road with held a cup like that, in a world that was not this one."

choices.text: Ask who they think you are

effects.log: {pw_hv_god} tells you about someone they knew in another life: how they met, the long road, the night by the fire when everything changed. You know none of it. Every word sounds like something you dreamed once and lost.

choices.text: Tell them gently that you are a stranger

effects.log: {pw_hv_god} nods and looks away. Later, when they think you are not looking, they watch you cross the hall, all the way, with the face of someone hearing a song they used to know.

events.text: {pw_hv_god}, god of {pw_hv_domain}, has kept a scroll for longer than this heaven has had a floor: a faded portrait of someone they knew before they were a god. They have never shown it to anyone. Tonight they unroll it in front of you without a word. The face in it is not yours. The way it stands is.

choices.text: Look at the portrait a long time

effects.log: You look until the lamps burn low. When you hand it back, {pw_hv_god} rolls it up very carefully. "I am not mad," they say. "I know it is not you. I only wanted to see if you would look at it the way they used to look at the sea."

choices.text: Ask what became of the person in it

effects.log: "They saved my life," {pw_hv_god} says. "Then they went on, the way they always did, to the next road, the next life. I kept their name in a book so I would not lose it. And one day I found I was written in that book myself."

choices.text: Offer to sit for a new portrait

effects.log: {pw_hv_god} laughs, a little wet. "I will paint you," they say, "and hang you beside them. If I am wrong, no harm done." The portrait takes a season. When it is finished the two hang side by side, and visitors to the hall keep stopping in front of them without knowing why.

events.text: Something cold comes fast down a corridor of mist, and before you can move, {pw_hv_god}, god of {pw_hv_domain}, has stepped in front of you with their arms out, the way a person shields someone they have shielded many times before. The cold thing passes. The god lowers their arms and looks at them, baffled. 'Why did I do that?' they say. 'I do not even know you.'

choices.text: "Perhaps you did, once."

effects.log: {pw_hv_god} laughs uncertainly. "Perhaps," they say. "I knew someone, long ago, who was always walking into trouble. I stood in front of them so often it became a habit. I suppose a habit can outlive the person."

choices.text: Thank them, and promise to return it someday

effects.log: "Nobody returns those," {pw_hv_god} says. But a season later, when a storm comes through the hall, you are the one who steps in front, and the god stands behind you looking very strange, as if a long debt had been paid in the wrong direction.

choices.text: Ask about the one they used to protect

effects.log: "Stubborn," {pw_hv_god} says. "Kind to the wrong people. Always climbing something." They look at you sidelong. "You are not them. But you would have liked each other."

events.text: In one of the seats of {pw_hv_tier} sits {pw_hv_self}, a lesser god of {pw_world}, who was born in it once, climbed it, and chose to stay. When you come in they look up, and their face is not your face, and it is: the way a river is the same river further down. 'Ah,' says {pw_hv_self}. 'There you are. I wondered if you would come.'

choices.text: Ask what they are to you

effects.log: "The last time," says {pw_hv_self}. "Or one of the times. We climbed this far once, you and I, and I sat down. I have always wondered what you would choose instead."

choices.text: Ask whether they were happy, choosing to stay

effects.log: {pw_hv_self} thinks about it honestly, which you like. "Most days," they say. "It is good work, and I am still in the world I love. But I sat down before the top. I never saw the throne up close. Go and look at it for me."

choices.text: Sit beside them a while, saying nothing

effects.log: You sit. It is the easiest silence of your life. When you rise to go, {pw_hv_self} touches your sleeve. "Mind the forty-first step," they say, and you both laugh, and neither of you can say why.

events.text: {pw_hv_self}, a lesser god of {pw_world}, comes to find you, which gods do not do. They carry a bowl of still cloud and set it between you, and in it two faces float side by side: yours, and theirs. 'I remember being you,' says {pw_hv_self}, 'a little. The way you remember a house you lived in when you were small. Do you remember being me?'

choices.text: Look into the bowl and try

ok.log: For one moment you remember it all: the climb, the empty seat, the choice to sit. It was a good choice. It is not yours. {pw_hv_self} nods as if you had said so aloud.

fail.log: Nothing comes. {pw_hv_self} is not disappointed. "Better," they say. "It means you are new. I was afraid you would only be me again."

choices.text: Say you do not, and that you are sorry

effects.log: "Do not be sorry," says {pw_hv_self}. "I would not want to be remembered too well. It would make it hard for you to be anyone else."

choices.text: Ask what they know of the one who made this world

effects.log: "More than the others," {pw_hv_self} says, "and less than you will. I only know this: every time I look at the empty throne, it looks back like someone waiting to hear their own name."

events.text: The lamps of {pw_hv_tier} gutter all at once, and the gods go quiet in their seats. Something is walking the halls: the false god of {pw_world}, the one that rose against this heaven and took the temples below for its own. It is tall as a pillar, made of shadow and stripped temple gold, and it is sniffing the air. 'Something new,' it says, in a voice like a coin dropped down a well. 'Something that smells of the stairs.' It is looking for you.

choices.text: Hide behind a pillar and watch it

effects.log: It passes so close you could touch the gold. Up close it is patched together: a temple bell here, a shrine's crown there, prayers it took that were meant for someone else. It does not see you. It will be back.

choices.text: Step out and let it see you

ok.log: It looks at you a long time. Then, for the first time in an age, it is the false god who steps back. "Later," it says, and the lamps come up again.

fail.log: It strikes once, almost lazily, and you are flung across the hall. "Later," it says. "I do like a hunt."

choices.text: Lead the frightened gods out the back way

effects.log: You find the door the lamp-spirits use and take the gods through it one by one. The false god finds an empty hall and roars, and every stolen bell it is made of rings.

events.text: A god of {pw_hv_tier} comes to your door at night, trembling, and begs you to hide them. The false god of {pw_world} is hunting the halls, they whisper. It was one of them once, seated like the rest, until the one who made them all went silent, and it decided the silence meant the seat at the top was free. Now it wants the throne. And somebody has told it that a stranger has come up the stairs who might be climbing toward it.

choices.text: Hide the god in your own room

effects.log: You sit up all night by the door. Toward dawn the false god goes by in the corridor, slowly, gold dust falling from it like snow, and stops outside, and goes on. It knows where you sleep now.

choices.text: Go and find it before it finds you

ok.log: You meet it at a crossing of corridors and hold it there until the gods have all got away. It is stronger than you. It is also, you notice, careful of you, as if you reminded it of something.

fail.log: It throws you into a wall of mist and stands over you, breathing. "Not yet," it says. "When you are higher. When it will mean something."

choices.text: Ask who told it about you

effects.log: The god does not know. But in the morning you notice {pw_hv_rival} watching you from across the court with an odd, unhappy face.

events.text: The false god has been hunting you for a season, and you have learned its ways: it cannot cross running cloud, it hates the sound of an honest prayer, and wherever it goes it leaves gold dust that is not gold. Tonight you find its den in a forgotten corner of {pw_hv_tier}: a heap of stolen temple bells, and in the middle of them, asleep, the thing itself. On a nail by the door hangs a name-board from a god's seat, old and cracked. The name on it has been scratched out.

choices.text: Read the name under the scratches

ok.log: It was a god once, of a small and gentle domain: Lost Things. Before the gold. You whisper the name. In its sleep, the false god turns over, like someone called from very far away.

fail.log: The board crumbles in your fingers. The false god stirs, and you are away down the corridor before it wakes, with a splinter of the board in your palm and the shape of a single letter.

choices.text: Ring one of the stolen bells to wake the heaven

effects.log: The bell rings across the whole heaven. Gods come from every hall, and for the first time they see the den for what it is: a heap of other people's prayers. The false god flees to a corner of the heaven it cannot easily leave.

choices.text: Leave a single honest prayer at the door, and go

effects.log: You pray, plainly, for the people below. The false god wakes with a cry and flees deeper into the heaven, into the one corner where it cannot run any further.

events.text: You corner the false god of {pw_world} at the edge of {pw_hv_tier}, where the cloud ends and there is nothing below but the long fall to the world. It turns at bay, huge and cracked, gold dust pouring from it like sand from a split sack. 'I waited,' it says. 'I waited {pw_years} years for the one who made us to come back. They never did. So I took the seat. Somebody had to.' It is very strong. It is also, you see now, very frightened.

choices.text: Let it go

effects.log: You step aside. It goes past you without a word, down into the dark of its stolen temples, and the heaven breathes again, for now.

choices.text: Speak the name that was scratched out

effects.log: You say its old name. The false god goes still. The gold falls off it like old leaves, and underneath is a small god of lost things who has been lost for a very long time. "Nobody has said that in an age," it whispers. "Will you tell them I am sorry?"

choices.text: Tell it the one who made them is closer than it thinks

ok.log: It looks at you, and something in its cracked face believes you, though you hardly know why you said it. The stolen gold slides off it in a heap. What is left sits down on the cloud, small and grey, and waits.

fail.log: It laughs, a cracked and terrible laugh, and goes over the edge of the cloud, down into the world, where its temples are.

choices.text: Fight it, here, at the edge

ok.log: You meet it at the edge and do not give a step, and at last the stolen gold cracks off it all at once and falls down through the clouds like a shower of sparks. What is left is small and grey and very tired. It sits down on the cloud and weeps.

fail.deathCause: the false god of the world you were born in
fail.log: It throws you down at the very edge and stands over you, and then, with a terrible effort, does not finish it. "Not yet," it says, and is gone.

events.text: Among the heaven's own immortals, the ones who climbed here from {pw_world} long before you and were let stay, is {pw_hv_rival}, who is used to being the newest and the best. They meet you on a narrow cloud bridge between two halls and do not step aside. 'So you are the one the gods are whispering about,' they say, grinning. 'I climbed for four hundred years to get this high. You did it in one life. Let us see what you are made of, stair-climber.'

choices.text: Step aside and let them pass

effects.log: {pw_hv_rival} looks almost disappointed. "Polite," they say. "We will see how long that lasts." They go on across the bridge, whistling.

choices.text: Do not step aside

ok.log: They shove, and you do not move. {pw_hv_rival} laughs out loud. "Oh, good," they say. "Something to do at last."

fail.log: They tip you off the bridge, quite gently, onto a cloud a little below. "Lesson one," they call down. "This bridge is mine."

choices.text: Ask what four hundred years up here is like

effects.log: The grin slips, for a breath. "Long," says {pw_hv_rival}. "You will see." Then it is back, and they push past you.

events.text: {pw_hv_rival} has been busy. Word has gone round {pw_hv_tier} that the stranger from the stairs is a spy for the false god, or a thief come to rob the Jade Vault, or both. Gods who greeted you last season look away now. You find {pw_hv_rival} by the spring where the immortals bathe, telling the story again to anyone who will listen, with a great many gestures.

choices.text: Answer them in front of everyone

ok.log: You answer every charge with a plain fact until the crowd is laughing, and not at you. {pw_hv_rival} goes red to the ears. "This is not over," they say, and everyone agrees that it is not.

fail.log: They are better at this than you. By the end the crowd is sure of nothing except that you lost your temper. {pw_hv_rival} bows, smiling.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let your deeds answer

effects.log: You go on helping the gods with their small troubles and say nothing. Within a season the story has gone sour in the mouth of anyone who tells it. {pw_hv_rival} is furious, and does not know at what.

choices.text: Find out why they are so afraid of you

effects.log: An old lamp-spirit tells you. {pw_hv_rival} has climbed every tier there was to climb, and tried for four hundred years to reach the empty throne at the top, and never could. They think you have come to do what they could not.

events.text: The Jade Vault is robbed: a jar of unsung songs is gone from its shelf. Quill, its keeper, is in despair, and every eye in heaven turns to the stranger from the stairs. Then you find the jar, tucked half out of sight in your own room, where you did not put it. In the dust beside it is a footprint you know: the light, quick step of {pw_hv_rival}.

choices.text: Take the jar back to Quill and say nothing of the footprint

effects.log: Quill is so relieved they ask no questions. Across the Vault {pw_hv_rival} watches you hand it back, and something in their face changes, and they do not know what to do with it.

choices.text: Take the jar back and name the thief

effects.log: The gods believe you, at last. {pw_hv_rival} is barred from the Vault for a hundred years. They meet your eyes across the court, and what is in theirs is worse than anger: they look ashamed.

choices.text: Take the jar to {pw_hv_rival} instead

effects.log: You put it in their hands. "You dropped this," you say. {pw_hv_rival} stares at the jar, and at you. "Why?" they say. You find you do not know, except that four hundred years is a long time to be the newest thing in heaven.

events.text: {pw_hv_rival} challenges you at last, properly, before the whole heaven, on the narrow cloud bridge where you first met, over the long drop to {pw_world}. 'One of us goes on up,' they say. 'One of us goes back down the stairs. I have waited four hundred years. I will not wait behind you.' The gods have come out to watch. Pell, the sweeper of the stairs, is in the front row, holding their broom like a banner.

choices.text: Refuse: there is room above for both of you

effects.log: The heaven goes very quiet. {pw_hv_rival} looks at you as if you had spoken another language. "There is one throne," they say. "Then go and sit on it, if it will have you," you say. "I will not stop you." They do not move for a long time.

choices.text: Race them up the next stair instead

ok.log: You take the stair three steps at a time and reach the top one step ahead, and turn, and offer them your hand up the last step. {pw_hv_rival} takes it. "Fine," they say, out of breath and almost laughing. "Fine. You are faster."

fail.log: They are four hundred years lighter on these stairs than you. At the top they turn and look down at you, and do not gloat, which surprises you both.

choices.text: Fight on the bridge

ok.log: It is a long, hard, clean fight, and at the end of it {pw_hv_rival} is sitting on the bridge, and you are holding out your hand. They look at it a long time before they take it. "Up, then," they say. "Go on. Somebody should."

fail.log: They know this bridge better than you ever will. You end on your back at the edge, looking at the world far below. {pw_hv_rival} does not push. "Not today," they say, breathing hard, and walk away.

events.text: A storm comes up from the world below, the worst in an age, and tears through {pw_hv_tier}. When it has passed, word comes that {pw_hv_rival} was caught on the old cloud bridge when it broke, and is clinging to what is left of it over the long drop, and none of the gods can reach that far. They came up here from {pw_world}, the way you did. They can fall the way you can.

choices.text: Run for the gods: it is not your fall to take

effects.log: By the time the gods have made a chain of hands, {pw_hv_rival} has dragged themself back alone, torn and furious and alive. They do not thank anyone. They do look for you in the crowd.

choices.text: Throw them a rope of your own qi

ok.log: You pour your qi into a line of light and it holds, and they climb it hand over hand. On the far side {pw_hv_rival} sits a long time with their head down. "I would have let you fall," they say at last. "Once." In front of the whole heaven they name you the better of the two.

fail.log: The line of light thins and snaps, but it buys them the moment they need to swing up onto the last of the bridge. They are safe. They know who to thank, and it costs them visibly.

choices.text: Go out along the broken bridge yourself

ok.log: You reach them on the last strand of cloud and haul them back. Afterwards {pw_hv_rival} kneels before the whole heaven and says your name, plainly, as the better of the two of you. Nobody has ever heard them say anything plainly before.

fail.deathCause: the long fall from the heaven of the world you were born in
fail.log: The strand gives under you both. The wolves of the god of the Wild catch you at the very edge, by your collars, like pups. {pw_hv_rival} is safe. You are not well for a long time.

events.text: From the edge of {pw_hv_tier} you part the cloud with one hand and look down. On a plain of {pw_world} two armies are drawing up: {pw_hv_war}, at war again. From up here they are very small. You can see what neither of them can: the river they are fighting over would carry water enough for both, if one old dam were opened, high in the hills where nobody goes.

choices.text: Close the cloud. It is not your place

effects.log: You let the cloud close over the plain. You do not sleep that night, and you hear, or think you hear, the battle far below.

choices.text: Go down in the night and open the dam

ok.log: You climb down through the clouds and put your shoulder to the old stones. By dawn the river is running high on both sides of the plain. The armies stand looking at it, and then at each other, and then, slowly, they go home.

fail.log: The old stones will not shift for you. You are still straining at them when you hear the armies meet on the plain below.

choices.text: Send the same dream to both generals

ok.log: That night both generals dream the same dream: the dam, the river, a stranger's voice. In the morning they meet under a white cloth, very embarrassed, and the war is over by noon.

fail.log: One general dreams it. The other does not. The battle comes anyway, smaller than it might have been.

events.text: The war between {pw_hv_war} has gone on for years. Tonight, looking down through the cloud, you see a child of one people lost in the hills near the camp of the other. A sentry has seen the child too, and is standing very still with a spear, not sure what to do. From up here you are the only one who can see the whole of it.

choices.text: Make the sentry's lantern gutter, so the child slips by

effects.log: The lantern dims; the child creeps past in the dark and is home by morning. The sentry never knows. It is a kindness. It is not enough to end a war.

choices.text: Light the child's way straight to the sentry's fire

ok.log: The sentry takes the child in, feeds them, and in the morning walks them across the lines under a white cloth. Someone on the other side, watching, lowers a spear. It starts there. By spring the war is over, and nobody can say quite how.

fail.log: The sentry takes the child in and sends them home in the morning. Nobody on the other side sees it. The war goes on, a little smaller in one heart.

choices.text: Go down yourself and walk the child home

effects.log: You walk out of the night and take the child's hand. The sentry lowers the spear and stares. In the camps afterwards both peoples tell of the stranger who came out of the hills, and both claim them.

events.text: Far below it is the Feast of the Maker, and the people of {pw_world} are lighting paper lanterns and sending them up toward the sky. From {pw_hv_tier} you watch them come: thousands of small lights, rising and rising, and going out one by one long before they reach the cloud. Not one has ever arrived. Tonight one of them is still burning when it touches the edge of heaven, right by your hand.

choices.text: Catch it

effects.log: It is a lantern of {pw_people}, badly made, and on it in a child's hand is written: "Are you there?" You keep it. You do not know what else to do with it.

choices.text: Breathe on it and send it higher

effects.log: It goes on rising, past {pw_hv_tier}, up toward the top of the heaven, toward a place nobody goes. You watch until you lose it. You think it arrived.

choices.text: Send a single light back down

effects.log: You fold a spark of your own qi into a lantern and let it fall. Far below, a village sees a light come down out of heaven for the first time in {pw_years} years. The priests will talk about it for a century.

events.text: Looking down through the cloud you find a temple of {pw_world} where an old priest is carving the first law of the world over the door, as they do every hundred years when the old carving wears away: {pw_law}. The priest's hands are not steady any more. One letter is going badly. Nobody else will ever notice. The priest will.

choices.text: Steady the priest's hand from above

effects.log: You breathe out, very gently, and the chisel goes true. The priest finishes the line, steps back, and bursts into tears without knowing why. The novices say afterwards the carving is the finest in a thousand years.

choices.text: Let the letter go wrong

effects.log: The letter comes out crooked. The priest looks at it a long time, then laughs, and leaves it. "Let them know a person carved it," the priest tells the novices. You decide that is better than anything you could have done.

choices.text: Read the law until you know why it was the first

effects.log: You read it all day. It is such a small law. It is the kind of thing a person decides on a quiet evening, hoping it will be enough. You find you know exactly which evening.

events.text: The priests of {pw_world} teach that its maker {pw_record}. Tonight, from the edge of {pw_hv_tier}, you watch a philosopher in the market of {pw_kingdom} argue that there was never any maker at all, and a priest argue back, and the crowd throw onions at both of them. It is the most alive you have seen anything look in a long time.

choices.text: Laugh until you have to sit down

effects.log: The gods nearby look at you oddly. You do not care. Far below, the onions run out, and the priest and the philosopher go off together for supper, still arguing.

choices.text: Send the philosopher a small sign

effects.log: A single onion rolls to the philosopher's feet, already sprouting. They pick it up, frown at the sky, put it in a pocket, and argue a little less certainly after that.

choices.text: Leave them to it: it is a good argument

effects.log: A world that can argue about its maker, you think, does not need one standing over it. The thought is oddly comforting, and oddly sad.

events.text: A year in the Ninth Heaven, and you have not gone near the throne. Tonight you do. Pell is sweeping the last step, and stops when you come. 'I swept every step of this heaven waiting for whoever it is for,' Pell says. They take the old chisel out of its cloth and lay it on the arm of the throne. On the stone beneath it someone long ago cut a single chisel scratch, the mark a maker leaves to say: mine. Nobody has ever sat here. The stone is warm.

choices.text: "Not yet."

effects.log: You step back down. Pell nods and goes on sweeping, unhurried. "It has waited {pw_years} years," they say. "It can wait for you to finish thinking."

choices.text: Refuse it, and keep a mortal heart

effects.log: You give Pell back the chisel. Pell looks at you a long moment and puts it away, without disappointment. "Then the forty-first step will just have to rock," they say.

choices.text: Take one of the gods' empty seats instead

effects.log: You turn from the throne and go down to the ring of the gods' seats, where some places are still empty. Pell follows, sweeping, and says nothing, and it feels like being walked home.

choices.text: Pick up the chisel, and sit

effects.log: The chisel fits your hand as if it had been worn to it. You climb the three low steps and turn, and sit.

events.text: When you come at last to the empty throne, the gods of {pw_world} have climbed up behind you, every one, and stand in a ring in the hall with no walls: the warm ones and the cold ones, the healer and the old soldier, the keeper of the lanterns. Nobody speaks. Below, in every temple, the people who love their maker are praying tonight, as they always do, and for once you can hear every word. Every prayer is the same. 'Come home.'

choices.text: "Not yet."

effects.log: You step back. Nobody stops you. The gods go quietly back down to their seats, and below the prayers go on, patient, as they have for {pw_years} years.

choices.text: Refuse, gently: let them love a maker who is not here

effects.log: "They have loved an empty chair for {pw_years} years," you say, "and it has made them kind. Let it stay empty." The god of the Hearth, at the back, is crying, and you cannot tell which way.

choices.text: Take an empty seat among the gods

effects.log: You walk down into the ring. The gods make room, without being asked, the way a family moves along a bench.

choices.text: Sit, and answer the prayers

effects.log: You climb the three low steps. Behind you, one by one, the gods of {pw_world} kneel.

events.text: The people of {pw_world} have stopped praying to their maker. In the temples below the old altars are cold, and the priests teach that whoever made the world went away and left it to suffer, and should never be let back. You can hear them from the Ninth Heaven. You stand at the foot of the empty throne, and understand that whoever sits in it will be sitting in the seat of the most hated thing in the world.

choices.text: "Not yet."

effects.log: You turn away for now. The hall is very cold tonight. Far below, a priest is telling a crowd that nothing up here deserves their love, and you find you cannot entirely disagree.

choices.text: Refuse it: they are right not to want a maker back

effects.log: You leave the throne to the dark. Let the world belong to the people who stayed in it. It is the first thing up here that has felt entirely like your own choice.

choices.text: Take a lesser seat, and help them without being hated

effects.log: A small god of a small domain can do a great deal of good, if nobody knows to curse it. You go down to the ring of seats.

choices.text: Sit anyway, and come home to a world that does not want you

effects.log: You climb the three low steps. Somebody has to answer for the silence. You sit.
